utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Do you have something to raise, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Will the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, my full name is Dean Paul Manning, M-a-n-n-i-n-g.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What's your current job?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm a member of the Australian Federal Police and I'm the currently the senior police liaison officer based in Dubai in the United Arab Emirates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: How long have you been a member of the Australian Federal Police?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I joined the Australian Federal Police in 1983. I served predominantly in Canberra. I also served with the United Nations in Cyprus, and in 1998 I served here at the Tribunal for six years. I've also worked for United Nations Oil-for-Food inquiry in New York and returned to my police service in 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The six years that you were at the Tribunal you were an investigator with the Office of the Prosecutor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, for four years I was an investigator with the Srebrenica team, and for two years I was the team leader of the Croatia investigations team, predominantly involved in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you describe your duties and responsibilities for that four years when you were an investigator on the Srebrenica team.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was a senior investigator involved in all aspects of the investigation, including taking witness statements, interviewing suspects, witnesses, and generally obtaining or verifying evidence, but my primary duties was liaison with the Srebrenica exhumations and autopsy project which was occurring in Bosnia. I liaised with the exhumations autopsy team and ultimately assisted the experts in that process in preparing their reports for presentation to the Court, and I also summarised the work of the teams in the field and presented evidence in relation to several trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you describe -- can you describe in a little bit more detail exactly what you did in this role, which sites you went to, which particular items you examined. Give us an idea of that.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was tasked with co-ordinating the activities of the investigations team with the exhumation autopsy teams. Those teams were run by experts in their field, and I provided whatever assistance they would require, which also meant monitoring the exhumation process and the work at the mortuary. I visited all the sites connected to Srebrenica, including all the execution points and all the mass graves, either after they'd been exhumed, whilst they were being exhumed, or after. I visited and was present at the -- at the exhumation of 11 mass graves, and over a period of six years I also visited those graves on a regular basis, including when the Bosnian commission for missing persons was exhuming those graves. My role was also to examine the evidence that was being obtained from that process. I examined all the physical artefacts that were recovered from the process in the field and in the mortuary. This included shell casings, blindfolds, ligatures, identification documents, and material that showed a link not only to the identity of the victims but connections to Srebrenica, connections to their killing in 1995, and connections to DutchBat and also items which, as I said, showed identification of the victims but also their religious affiliation, that being Muslim or Islamic religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you tell us what types of experts were engaged by the OTP in this process and the experts that you liaised with.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The exhumations team was normally headed by an archaeologist, anthropologist, and he or she would have a number of archaeologists, anthropologists at the grave sites. There would also be surveying experts, police photographers, police evidence handling officers. At the mortuary there were anthropologists, forensic dentists, X-ray experts. And during the course of the investigation, we also employed experts such as ballistics examiners who examined the shell cases from the primary and secondary mass graves and were able to make links between those sites. We also -- and I also worked with soil expert who examined soil from the mass graves and the areas connected to executions. We also had cloth, explosives, and DNA experts who examined material from the mass graves and the autopsy process. We also had expert forensics teams examine some of the execution points and an horologist who examined watches found on the bodies within the mass graves. I worked with all those experts. I helped them in providing material and access to sites. I took them to the sites. I took material to them. I reviewed their expert reports and I summarised those expert reports for presentation in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The ICTY's forensic programme ran from 1996 to 2001; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: How many mass graves were identified during this period that were suspected to be Srebrenica related?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, there were 43 mass graves directly connected to Srebrenica during that part of the investigation, and I can say that they -- that is a conservative numbering process. Some graves were made up of sub-graves, for instance, Glogova, but we would take a conservative view and number that grave as one large grave. So 43 mass graves in total, including primary and secondary, but that numbering system was somewhat arbitrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many of those graves were exhumed by the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: We exhumed all the primary mass graves, 13 mass graves, and another -- in total, I think we exhumed 22 mass graves, some of which were -- had been robbed, such as Cancari Road -- sorry, Zeleni Road, Zeleni Jadar 2 mass grave and Hodzici 1 mass grave, which we believed had not been used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What happened to those other graves that had been identified but not exhumed by the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, a decision was taken in 2000, 2001, to hand over responsibilities for the unexhumed graves to the Bosnian commission for missing persons who were then asked by the Tribunal to exhume -- remove the bodies from the graves, and that team was monitored by the independent commission for missing persons -- International Commission for Missing Persons, ICMP, and for part of 2001, the ICTY monitored the exhumation of those graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did you personally monitor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Thank you. Now you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, did you personally monitor any of those exhumations done by the Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honours. In fact, I was responsible for drafting the agreement and setting the process into place. It was eventually agreed to by the Prosecutor. I was present at the examination of the Ravnice 1 and 2 mass grave, primary mass grave, with the Bosnian commission for missing persons, with ICMP and with a very small team of ICTY staff. I was also present during the exhumation of Cancari Road 11, and over the next two years I would visit sites as my travel in Bosnia permitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, are you aware in addition to the graves that were handed over to the Bosnian authorities by the ICTY, are you aware whether they -- those authorities have located and exhumed any additional graves which are suspected to be Srebrenica related?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know that the Bosnian commission and ICMP have continued to not only exhume the graves we handed over but locate further graves which have been connected to Srebrenica, Bljeceva and other areas, and I understand that their work with DNA has provided definitive links to the Srebrenica missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, you have written three reports in 2000, 2001, and 2003 which summarised the findings of the various experts who were engaged by the OTP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. Those summary reports also included details of my own examinations of the artefacts and sites as well as a combination of the reports which were conducted -- created by the experts and were limited to a certain period of time. So I linked those expert reports from the first exhumation process up until 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, those are 65 ter numbers 2478, 2479, and 3937, and I'd like to tender them now if I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before -- you don't have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I actually do have an objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we hear from you first. Mr. Robinson, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, it's our belief that to admit an expert report through the testimony of a non-expert witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what is tendered is an expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's quoting from expert reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, we'll hear from that, yes. Let's continue. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Anyway, it's our position that to admit either portions of or an entire expert report through another witness violates the provisions Rule 94 bis. You've previously held that Rule 94 bis is lex specialis with respect to reports when deciding that you would not admit any of them under Rule 92 bis, and we think that the same principle would apply. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Can I hear from you, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Certainly. First, Mr. President, we're not tendering any expert reports through Mr. Manning. Mr. Manning has relied on two types of expert reports as source material for his report. One are the reports of the archaeologists, the anthropologists, and the pathologists who have already testified here at trial and those reports were already in evidence. There's a second set of reports that Mr. Manning has relied on the conclusions from and has cited those conclusions in his report, and I would submit that Mr. Manning relying on those conclusions -- or his evidence relying on those conclusions is admissible for three reasons. First, he has very clearly identified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you be more significant as regards the second set of reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes. I think, Mr. President, there's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you referring to 2479?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: 2479 is Mr. Manning's report, and in that he cites to a number of underlying reports, the ballistic evidence, the horologist report, the results of the examination of Pilica Dom and the Kravica warehouse, the soil analysis report and the textiles report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In which he participated?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No. They are independent expert reports which reached a conclusion about the particular artefacts they were examining, and Mr. Manning cites to that conclusion. Mr. President, the expert reports are very clearly identified. This was also -- this very issue was litigated in the Popovic case and the Trial Chamber there said that Mr. Manning was entitled to rely on the conclusion of reports that were not before the Trial Chamber, and in these circumstances the fact that the underlying source reports weren't in evidence would ultimately go to the weight of Mr. Manning's evidence, and that was at transcript page 18996 of the Popovic case. The last point I'd like to make is most, if not all, of the conclusions that Mr. Manning's relying on are already recognised as adjudicated facts in this case, and I can point you to adjudicated facts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before you -- it's okay. Could you give me by way of example, probably my understanding is that he's also rely -- one of the materials he's relying on is US naval criminal investigative reports. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, correct. He does cite to that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's take the last one --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms report. Could you give an example how he's relying on that report in his report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Certainly. Mr. Manning, what his role was to send the shell casings away to that bureau to analyse to see if they were matches. They reported back in a report and said the following shell casings indicate they came from the same gun. Mr. Manning has taken those results and interpreted them and said those shell casings came from these. There are match shell casings from particular sites and then he has drawn a conclusion of what that means to have shell casings fired from the same gun coming from a particular site. For example, there are shells fired from the same gun that appear at Orahovac and then at Hodzici Road 3, 4, and 5, but Mr. Manning just simply takes the conclusion that these shell casings match and then he interprets that. But that conclusion that there are matching shell casings is also -- has been recognised as an adjudicated fact as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was waiting for the conclusion of French translation. So in a nutshell, Mr. Manning sent all those shell casings he collected to that US institution and he received the report from that institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And how about the US naval criminal investigative reports on Kravica and Pilica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Those two sites were processed by the NCIS in 1996, and they took two sets of samples from -- from those two particular sites. They took swabs of suspected human remains and swabs of suspected explosive residue. Those samples were provided to the Office of the Prosecutor, and then they were sent away to the Dutch forensic institute for processing to see what results there would be. Mr. Manning describes simply that these samples were taken by the NCIS, they were sent away, they were analysed by the Dutch forensic institute, and then these are the results that came back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A Dutch forensic report and US report the same one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No, they're different, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You talked about this related to Dutch forensic report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct. There is a report which is just the processing at the site at Pilica Dom, a report about the processing of Kravica warehouse and then there is a completely separate report from the Dutch forensic institute about where they analysed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just deal with it -- with it one by one. So US report, the US naval and criminal investigative reports on Kravica and Pilica was based upon the material collected during the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: During the on-site investigation in 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. How is Dutch forensic report related to the investigation at the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The samples that were taken by the, NCIS were given to the Office of the Prosecutor. The Office of the Prosecutor then sent them away to the Dutch forensic institute to be analysed. So those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you said NCIS were given to the Office of the Prosecutor. What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The naval criminal investigative service took those samples in 1996 from those sites and provided the samples to the Office of the Prosecutor, the physical samples of suspected explosive residue and suspected human remains. Then the Office of the Prosecutor sent those samples to the Dutch forensic institute, who came back and said -- for example, at the Pilica Dom I think there were 15 suspected explosive residue samples taken. One of them came back from the Dutch forensic institute as positive. So it's just two -- two different aspects of the one analysis of the same sample.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there any other reports than those I mentioned that Mr. Manning is relying on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think everything Mr. Manning relies on is -- I think, Professor Wright's reports are summarised, so all the six experts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm mentioning those evidence which is not in evidence before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: He has cited to conclusions by Professor Antony Brown who is the soil expert, and I believe there are two of those reports. He has cited to a Dutch forensic institute report on the explosive residue taken from the Pilica Dom and Kravica warehouse. He's cited to a Dutch forensic institute report on the blood samples collected from those sites and the Grbavci school, a study of watches by Mr. Mark Mills, a Dutch forensic institute textile report on the ligatures and blindfolds, a US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms report on the Kravica warehouse -- sorry, report on shell casings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That's what -- included in what I mentioned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The two NCIS reports on the Kravica warehouse and the Pilica Dom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And if I could just mention, Mr. President, most of these conclusions have been recognised as adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give me an example -- examples of conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I can give you -- adjudicated fact 1703 says: "Investigation into the cartridges discovered at the grave site revealed that the cartridges found in the grave itself matched with those found along the road at the grave side, indicating that the victims in the grave were shot at the grave site." That's an adjudicated fact about Cerska. And if we go to adjudicated fact 1717, the OTP -- this is about Kravica warehouse: "The OTP sent a team of experts to examine the Kravica warehouse on 30 September 1996. Experts determined the presence of bullet strikes explosive residue, bullets and shell cases, as well as human blood, bones, and tissue adhering to the walls and floor of the building." And there's quite a few of -- facts like that. Number 1721, 1788, 1800, 1822, 1855, 1861, 1863, 1879, 1889 -- I think -- 1886, 1880 -- and 18 -- I think that's it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you like to reply, Mr. Robinson? Yes, Mr. Mitchell, do you have anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Nothing else to add, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Well, I would like to apply -- first of all, I would like to call your attention to the scheme of Rule 94 bis which envisions that expert findings will be presented to the Trial Chamber first by way of notice by the Prosecution, and then if the Defence challenges those, then they have the right to test them in court, and that was the basis your Ruling under 92 bis that experts reports wouldn't be admissible so the Defence would have a right to challenge them. So what's being done in this instance takes away our right to challenge those reports, since this witness could do nothing more than repeat the findings of the report. He's not an expert in any of those fields to be able to ask about the basis of those findings. So it's our position that this is the same rationale as you rejected the 92 bis experts that you should also reject admitting the findings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 92 bis expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. You said that they were -- you would not allow expert reports or expert testimony to be admitted by way of Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was speaking in a little shorthand. In any event, our first point is essentially by bringing them in through a witness other than the expert they're circumventing Rule 94 bis which is lex specialis. Secondly, I call your attention to the Barney Kelly decision in the Milosevic case about which I know you are very familiar with, and then they said that it was not proper for an investigator to come and repeat the information given to investigators in the field by witnesses, and essentially this is also what's going on here. This investigator is repeating the expert's conclusions, and we think that the decision to allow that would run afoul of the decision in the Milosevic case on the testimony of Barney Kelly. Finally with respect to adjudicated facts, we don't think -- although, first of all, we wonder why it's necessary for the Prosecution to introduce evidence when they have adjudicated facts on the very same point. Even if they're allowed to do that, we don't see how that would affect the admissibility. The question is whether evidence from an expert is admissible through the testimony of some other witness, and it's either admissible or it's not, and the question of whether those same pieces of information have been judicially noticed we think is not relevant on the issue of admissibility. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can respond very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Before that, could we agree upon the fact that Mr. Manning is not appearing as an expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's correct. Mr. Manning is not an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just very briefly. I think the Milosevic decision is very clear - this is the decision of 30 September 2002 - that summarising evidence is admissible, and what the decision says in paragraph 21, that in every case the basic issue is whether the material being summarised is itself admissible. And in this case, I would submit, it's clearly admissible. It's clearly identified by Mr. Manning. The second point I would make is Mr. Manning, while he necessarily refers to the conclusions of these experts, what the purpose of his testimony is is to explain or to put them into context how -- how those conclusion were is reached. So taking the shell casing example, where those shell casings came from, how they were sent, what was asked to be done, and then what those findings mean to say that shell casings from particular sites match; Mr. Manning then interprets that and turns it into -- or puts his own analysis on it and that's what he's presenting to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me be clear one thing about -- you are not tendering the report itself, for example, US Bureau of Alcohol Tobacco and Firearms report, or NCIS report, separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: They're not being tendered at all, Mr. President. Mr. Manning's three reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He's relying on those reports or he's citing the conclusion --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: He's citing to the conclusions of those reports, but we're not tendering the underlying expert reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How can you [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] source material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm overlapping. How would you distinguish from the submission of Mr. Robinson that by doing so we are encroaching the spirit of Rule 94 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that Rule applies to the expert reports themselves. I think Mr. Manning is entitled to cite -- so long as it's clearly identified, he's entitled to cite to another document so we know where his report is coming from, and I don't think that is circumventing Rule 94 at all, because we're not seeking to tender those underlying expert reports through him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell, he's entitled to cite and rely on the reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe he's entitled to cite those conclusions, clearly identify where they're coming from and rely on them and explain to them from his own investigative experience and analysis what those conclusions mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, turn to you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. In rebuttal to that, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm pausing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will hear from you, if anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just wanted to say how can you distinguish the findings from his testimony once -- because his testimony assumes that the findings are true. It goes -- for example, shell casings. It assumes that the shell casings match, before he can go on to explain what the significance of that is. So I don't see how the Prosecutor can make that distinction. There -- the results of the expert report are being assumed to be true; otherwise, his testimony is meaningless. So I think that that's a distinction without a difference in terms of the argument. Anyway, I'm ready to answer any questions you might have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For example, 65 ter number 2478 and 3937 are, in my understanding, summaries of forensic evidence by Dr. Wright, Peccerelli, Clark or Baraybar. As regards those part, given the complexity and technicality or the size themselves, would the Chamber not be assisted by hearing from Mr. Manning as to how to understand or how to read those voluminous evidence in a brief manner?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you do not oppose to that part?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Given that the evidence has already been admitted from the experts themselves, we don't oppose this witness assisting the Chamber with understanding that evidence, since we've had a chance to test it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the timing, the Chamber will take a break now, a bit early break. So we'll break for 25 minutes and resume -- we will resume at 3.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, having considered your submission and the fact that you do not object to the admission of two of the tendered reports, namely 65 ter numbers 2478 and 3937, the Chamber has decided to admit them into evidence. As discussed earlier, they simply refer to and summarises the reports already in evidence in this case which the accused has had an opportunity to challenge through the cross-examination of other experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to 65 ter 2479, Mr. Mitchell, the Chamber would like to know if there are any parts of that report that refer to reports or documents already in evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think a large -- the vast majority of that report cites to the archaeological, anthropological and pathology reports that are already in evidence. There's only selected portions of that report that cite to these other expert reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitchell. In that case, the Chamber has decided to admit only those portions of the report which refer to reports and documents already in evidence in this case. With respect to the remaining portions, the Chamber would like the Prosecution to redact those from the report. This, of course, assumes that the redactions would not make the whole report incomprehensible. If they do, the Prosecution should bring that to the Chamber's attention. In addition, the Chamber would allow the Prosecution to discuss with the witness his involvement in obtaining the information and the reports cited in 65 ter 2479. The Prosecution can then consider bringing the person or persons who prepared that information and produced the related reports. This will then enable the accused to challenge the findings in accordance with the Rules. That's the Ruling. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President, for that Ruling. I just want to point out that in 65 ter number 2478, on pages 5 and 6, there are references to the results of the Netherlands Forensic Institute textile report and then also the ballistics report on page 6. So I would ask that you apply the same Ruling for 2479 to those of 2478.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. The same Ruling will apply to that part as well. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, I want to ask you very briefly about two additional reports in addition to the three that we've been talking about. In 2005, you reviewed the work the Bosnian authorities and the ICMP and you produced two reports summarising their findings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I don't want to get into the details of those two reports, but can you just very briefly describe the process that you went through of reviewing the work of the Bosnians and the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, briefly, I was tasked with examining the records from the ICMP exhumations and also the DNA analysis conducted by the laboratories with the intention of identifying those records that they had of identified people which related to mass graves we had identified as being connected to Srebrenica. On the basis of that, I collated the figures and the numbers that they had presented for DNA identifications and linked those to the primary and secondary mass graves that the ICTY were aware were from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And is it correct that this process that you started in 2005 of analysing and reporting on this work has now been taken over by another investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And can you tell us the name of that other investigator?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't recall his last name, Dusan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Dusan Janc?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, I want to move to a different area now and discuss the blindfolds and ligatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 16274 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: First --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Before we move on, could we give the number to the reports we -- --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that caveat, there's no objection to the admission of those three.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 65 ter 02478 will be Exhibit P4502. 65 ter 03937 will be Exhibit P4503. And 65 ter 02479 will be P4504.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And in your notification that you were minded to -- you were alluding that you would tender the other expert reports but it's clear that you're not tendering them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I simply listed them in case I used them, but the intention was not to tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Now it's clear. Let's move on. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, can you tell us who made this chart and can you explain to us what it means.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I produced this chart, this table. The first part of the table is relating to ligatures and the then-exhumed mass graves, and the bottom table, which you can't see completely, is the same sort of table related to blindfolds. Because the blindfolds and ligatures were located not only during the exhumation but at the autopsy and examination of the body, the reports from, for instance, Professor Wright would list a number of blindfolds for a grave but he would acknowledge in his report that that was not a complete listing, and the same for the mortuary, because by the time the bodies had arrived, on occasions the blindfolds or ligatures had either fallen off the body or the body had become disassociated. I physically examined every item that was listed as a blindfold or a ligature or could have been a blindfold or a ligature. I physically examined the item. I then sought the documentation for that item such as a photograph in situ on a body, the associated photographic logs, the evidence logs, the autopsy reports, observations by pathologists, crime scene officers and other experts. And I then made account of the blindfolds, where they were located, from what graves, and produced this table to -- to indicate the conservative numbering of how many blindfolds and how many ligatures were located within the graves, where they were located within the grave and which graves they were located in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, the details of each specific blindfold and ligature is in your three reports; is that right? The 2000, 2001, and 2003 reports.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Associated with each of those reports was annexes which had the listing of the blindfolds and the ligatures, including the photographic references, including photographs in situ on the body in the mortuary, and also linked to those three reports were the expert reports which included the autopsy and exhumation accounts related to those blindfolds and ligatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Mitchell, again. There's an administrative matter to consult the parties. utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yeah. Hopefully we're able to finish today, but if not, he could only go for, I imagine, a couple of hours at the most in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have -- given the Ruling we just made, would it be, by any chance, possible on the part of the Defence to conclude the cross-examination by today? But before that, how long would it take for your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I probably have half an hour left, maybe 45 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson or Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, but indeed there are a great many details that reveal the essence of the matter, and these details have to be presented, and they have to be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That doesn't tell us how many hours you need for your cross. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whatever the time may be allotted to the Defence, we'll stick to the original plan in terms of sitting. We are sitting tomorrow in the morning. Yes. Let's continue, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So, Mr. Manning, just to be clear, the conclusion of the numbers in this table, the total of 423 ligatures and 448 blindfolds, they're your numbers?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, very much. If you took the expert reports - particularly Richard Wright, Professor Haglund, Professor Clark and others - if you look at the number of blindfolds and ligatures in those reports, they were not the same and they were not these numbers. These are the result of my examination of -- of all aspects of the exhumation autopsy process over the period 1996 to 2001, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, just sticking with your 2000 report for a minute, there are two volumes of photographs that go with that report, is that correct, which show there's a photograph of each blindfold and each ligature?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender those two volumes. That's 65 ter 23631 and 23632. We move to add them to our 65 ter list but they're a composite of four numbers that were already listed on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, they will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P4505 and 4506 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd also like to tender the chart that's on the screen in front of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4507, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can have 65 ter 23634 in e-court. And, Mr. President, this is a composite image that we also applied for leave to add to our 65 ter list, and it was incorrectly described in that request. This contains all the photographs from the 2000 report that are in those two volumes. It also contains the photographs from Mr. Manning's two subsequent reports. So this is -- this is a photograph of everything in those three reports. So we'd ask for leave to add that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you're going to ask some questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'll ask a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, if you can tell us --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask for something? Could they be numbered in the same way like in these books? They don't have the same numbers, so it's very hard to identify them. So can they have visible numbers, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At the moment I don't follow, but could you assist us, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure what Mr. Karadzic is asking, if he's asking for the artefact number of each of the photographs or if -- if he wants them numbered 1 through 448. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you deal with this chart with Mr. Manning first and then see what we can do about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: First, Mr. Manning, can you tell us who compiled this composite image?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I -- I compiled this image.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And even though we've just talked about it, can you tell us what's on it? Where are these artefacts from?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document itself is -- is a -- a poster-sized image. There's also one for ligatures. It shows a photographic image of each blindfold from each of the primary and the related secondary mass graves. So if you see the first label, it says, "Branjevo Farm, Pilica." There are two blindfolds, two separate blindfolds which were located at the Branjevo military farm. And then each of the images from Cancari Road 12 represent individual blindfolds, et cetera, et cetera, through all the primary and secondary mass graves. Some images show a blindfold within the grave loose. Others show a blindfold on the head after body, either at the mortuary or in the grave, and some show that a blindfold or ligature at the mortuary being photographed after it was cleaned, but each image shows a separate blindfold or ligature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this is a composite of images that we have already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What would be the point of this -- having this composite?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can answer that. This is actually -- it's additional. It contains some additional images which are not in the books. So, for example, Lazete 1 and Lazete 2C are contained in this composite, but they're not contained in the two volumes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The two volumes of -- his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct. The two volumes just go with the 2000 report. This composite image is all three reports. So there's certainly some overlap. Everything that's in those two volumes will be on this image, but because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is any images that we have this in composite image should appear in one of the forensic reports somewhere in our evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Many of them will. I couldn't guarantee that all of them would have made their way into a report of the pathologist or the archaeologist, but they certainly would have originated at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you haven't answered my question as to the point of having this composite image --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- in addition to images that we already have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The point is simply, Mr. President, these artefacts are the subject of specific challenge in this case, and we want you -- or we'd like to offer you images of every single one of them so you can analyse exactly what they are and reach that determination yourself and this is a way of putting every single blindfold and every single ligature in one place to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's continue. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we look at 65 ter 23635.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You mentioned a similar composite image of ligatures. Is this what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, this is the same type of image. It represents -- each photo is a single ligature from the mass graves. There's no duplication, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd like to tender those -- those two images, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. They will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P4508 and P4509 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And your reports list a number of other artefacts which were recovered from the graves, including identification documents and items of -- are believed to be of religious significance. Can you tell us why you considered it important to detail those particular groups of artefact?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The identification material including the documents, photographs, and artefacts were considered very important to the Tribunal in (a) connecting the mass graves to Srebrenica to July of 1995 and the events following the fall of Srebrenica. They were also very important to hopefully provide identification of the victims, for the forensic process but also for the families of the victims. And I would routinely examine items in the field and at the mortuary, and I would regularly attend the mortuary, examine all those items, physically examine them and examine the documentation with them. I would then decide which items were conveyed to the ICTY either for further examination such as the shell cases, blindfold and ligatures and the watches, or I would organise the return of those items that were appropriate to the Bosnian authorities to PHR, Physicians for Human Rights, who were seeking to identify the bodies. And in the case of the religious items, I examined all the artefacts that were obtained during the several-year process and sought to identify any religious or other groupings for those individuals whose -- who had owned those artefacts. I found a significant number of religious artefacts. The only religion that I could equate to those artefacts was Islam in the majority of cases. There was no items that showed a connection to any other religious group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, you describe in various parts of your reports some particular artefacts that were recovered from Glogova, Zeleni Jadar 5 and 6, and Ravnice. Can you first tell us a bit about the Ravnice grave and what -- what the artefacts were that were found at that location?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was present in the field when the Ravnice grave was first identified. I was also present when it was first exhumed as Ravnice 1, and then I was present the following year when Ravnice 2, which is effectively the same grave, was exhumed. I personally saw the artefacts that were located within the grave amongst the bodies. Those artefacts included items that were indistinguishable from items at the Kravica warehouse which is approximately 8 kilometres away from the Ravnice primary grave. Those items included pieces of the masonry and physical structure of the warehouse, painted pieces of concrete, pieces of metal, pieces of machinery, and in one instance a piece of foam painted lettering which was a positive physical match for a piece of the same signage which was on the Kravica warehouse. So effectively, a piece of a sign had been knocked off the Kravica warehouse and then had been transported to the Ravnice primary mass graves and was within the bodies, a group of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What about the artefacts at Glogova and Zeleni Jadar 5 and 6?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, I was present not only at the Kravica warehouse on numerous occasions, but I was present when Glogova 2 primary mass graves was opened and Glogova 1. I was present when Zeleni Jadar 5 was exhumed and opened, and I was present and located with the team Zeleni Jadar 6. In each of those primary and secondary graves, there were significant numbers of items that were indistinguishable from items at the Kravica warehouse. In effect, there were pieces of the warehouse in the primary mass graves of Glogova 1 and 2, and there were pieces of the warehouse in the secondary mass graves of Zeleni Jadar 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you tell us then, based on the presence of these particular artefacts, what's the connection or the sequence between the warehouse, Glogova, and the two graves at Zeleni Jadar, Zeleni Jadar 5 and 6?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The Kravica warehouse is an execution point where a significant number of prisoners were killed. Those -- the bodies of the victims were then transported from the warehouse by heavy machinery. In doing so, that heavy machinery knocked down part of the door and frame and wall of the warehouse. That material was transported with the bodies; in one group to the Ravnice prime mass graves and another group to the Glogova primary mass graves, which is about 8 kilometres from the Kravica warehouse. Several months later, the primary mass graves of Glogova 1 and 2 were opened, and some of the contents, that is the bodies, removed by heavy machinery, and those bodies were then transported to the newly created secondary mass graves along Zeleni Jadar Road, and they were located within Zeleni Jadar 5 and 6, and from my work with the Bosnian commission, I saw similar artefacts in the other Zeleni Jadar graves, 1 to 4, and also at the Ravnice site. They were all effectively connected. One was an execution point. Three were mass primary graves, and the remainder were mass secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter number 23633 in e-court. Mr. President, this is another exhibit which we asked to add to our 65 ter list. It's a composite book of images and maps, every one of which is individually already on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ah, yes. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that's granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, have you had an opportunity to review all of the aerials that are in this book?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did you -- or can you tell us, did you have an opportunity to review them during your investigation?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, we made great use of the aerial images provided by the US government. We used them to identify the primary and secondary mass graves. I used them on many, many occasions to assist in locating the graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go to image number 20 in the hard copy, 32 in e-court. Can you tell us what we're looking at in this image?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a composite of two images which have been overlapped. I was responsible for producing the overlapped images and the yellow marking on those images. They show that Zeleni Jadar secondary mass graves from Zeleni Jadar 1 through to 6; and, in fact, Zeleni Jadar 1 should be Zeleni Jadar 1A, and there is Zeleni Jadar 1B. I was present when we located that grave and probed its contents. So effectively, there are seven secondary mass graves in the Zeleni Jadar Road area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did you personally visit each of these sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I've been to every site. As I say, I was present when 1B was located. I've been present when Zeleni 2 was examined. I've been present when Zeleni Jadar 5 was opened. I've been present at 3 and 4 and examined the area, and I was present at and part of the exhumation of Zeleni Jadar 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page, image number 2133 in e-court. You mentioned there should be a Zeleni Jadar 1A and B. If I can get the usher to assist you, if you could describe that in more detail and mark the image if -- if need be.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a single image which is made up of two images side by side. That joint image was provided to the ICTY. I marked the right-hand pane Zeleni Jadar 1. The left-hand pane shows the area on the 7th of September, and you can see that by the 2nd of October two areas had been excavated, one marked Zeleni Jadar 1, and if you look at this area of the map, that is the grave site that we identified and probed and labelled Zeleni Jadar 1B. It hadn't previously been examined because it is believed to be within a heavily mined area. So we mined a path to the area and examined the mass graves. But you can see that on the 7th of September, 1995, there were no mass graves in the area, and by the 2nd of October, 1995, what we now know to be two mass graves had been created.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Are the two graves we see in the right-hand shot, were they opened or closed at the time this was taken?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not an expert in photo examinations, but from using these images, I believe that Zeleni Jadar 1 is open in -- in that view, and also Zeleni Jadar 1B. And having examined particularly 1B, it had a very small area. It was a trench cut into a flat area, and I believe that this shows the mass graves as they'd been created and opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you mark on the top one 1A, 1B on the bottom where you've circled and then initial and date it with today's date, the 6th of March.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This image will be admitted as a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4510, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While not important, do you have the date of the previous image, Mr. Mitchell, the image 20?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can go back a page in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The composite image that you compiled, Mr. Manning, do you know what date is depicted in those two composite images?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know from working on this document that those images were produced without the date on them, but they are effectively the same images that you see in the previous -- in the subsequent photographs. When we requested that image, the -- the dates were not included, but they were taken from the other images that you see following that. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you confirm this statement by Mr. Mitchell that this is a composite image that you compiled based upon the images provided to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go to page 22 in the hard copy, 34 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: In the previous image we were looking at Zeleni Jadar 1A and 1B on the 7th of September, the 2nd of October. And if you can now describe what we can see in this particular image.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, again a split view, and this shows a date range in October of 1995. If you look at the 18th of October on the left-hand pane, you can see, certainly in the hard copy, it looks that the graves are still at least not covered up, still open, and if you look at the right-hand pane on the 20th of October, 1995, you can see that the graves have been covered in. And from examination of these documents previously, I believe that you can see vehicle marks on the soil where heavy machinery has sealed up the graves and flattened the ground in both Zeleni Jadar 1A and 1B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you tell us about Zeleni Jadar 2? Was there anything significant about that particular grave?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Zeleni Jadar 2 was created very, very close to a small stream. In fact, it was on the edge of the stream.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Perhaps -- my apologies. Perhaps we could go over to the next page and at page 23 in the hard copy and 35 in e-court. I apologise for interrupting you. If you could then continue your explanation.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: When you -- when you see that image, you can see that the white stripe across the middle of both photographs is, in fact, a dirt roadway. The grave can be clearly seen on the right-hand pane, and if you like, where the tip of the arrow is is the area where the river or small creek is. That mass graves was in an area that I had -- I have seen flooded, and when it was examined by Professor Wright, he found that it contained some human remains, scattered human remains. I went to the site with Dr. Wright, and he advised me that it was his belief that that mass graves had been robbed, that is, that the bodies had been removed, and that it was an indication that there was somewhere a tertiary grave which contained those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Could we go to image 31 in the hard copy, 44 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And if you can explain what we're looking at in this particular image.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, this is an image which I created. It shows three separate photographs overlaid. It shows the Hodzici Road or the area we called Hodzici Road, and mass graves 1 through to 7, secondary mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did you visit all of these seven sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I did. I was present at one stage when the Bosnian commission were exhuming, I think Hodzici 7. I went to each of the sites with Dr. Wright and with other members of the team, and particularly we examined Hodzici 1, which Professor Wright believed to have been dug as a primary -- as a secondary mass graves and not utilised completely as a grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor Wright fully exhumed Hodzici Road 3, 4, and 5; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And are you aware of what the results of any subsequent examination of Hodzici Road 1 are?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: It's my understanding that the Bosnian commission and ICMP examined Hodzici Road 1 and, in fact, found a number of bodies within that grave. It had not been completed filled, but they did find a number of bodies connected to Srebrenica in that mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we go to image 42 in the hard copy and 56 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And just to be clear for the record, we're looking at an image with -- a summary image of mass graves for each of the individual graves in this book. There's a series of photos related to each grave; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. In each grave area I've tried to produce a similar document to show not only the aerial image but highlight the area of the graves. In this instance these are the Liplje Road secondary mass graves. Liplje 1 was connected to the dam at Petkovci. And, to my knowledge, another three mass graves connected to Srebrenica have been located in this road, and in fact by the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons, and in fact I was present when we examined an area with the commission which was later found to be a mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Is it Liplje 1 that's connected to the dam or on another site?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Sorry, Liplje 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to image 48 in the hard copy and 63 in e-court. And if you can explain again what we're looking at here.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In the same manner, I've tried to highlight to the Court the aerial images which show the secondary mass graves. I'm responsible for those yellow images being placed on the document. The red image was not placed there by myself. And I'm aware that a further mass grave was identified on Cancari Road, and it's numbers Cancari Road 13, and, in fact, it's closer to Cancari Road 1. I'm also aware that the Bosnian commission, when they exhumed these mass graves, named them in a different manner to us. So some of the mass graves on Cancari Road are called Kamenica, et cetera, by the Bosnian commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. I want to look at one particular example which the Trial Chamber is familiar with, and that's Cancari Road 12, but if I can start off -- if we can go to image 18 in the hard copy and 29 in e-court. And just to lay a little bit of background, in your 2000 report, at page 16, you say that the aerial imagery of Branjevo Farm was first released on the 21st of March, 1996; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And the grave was then exhumed later that same year by Dr. Haglund.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct, Dr. Haglund and his team from PHR exhumed a number of bodies from that primary mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If you can just briefly describe what we're looking at here on image number 18.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've -- I've been to the military farm on a number of occasions. If you look at the vertical line which runs from the top third of the document to a group of buildings and roadways, that's -- it's now -- it's now destroyed, but it was then a farm. It was, to my knowledge, a pig farm. It consisted of a number of farm buildings. And if you moved to the left of the image, there's trackways and paths of vehicles, and the area marked "Burial area" is in fact the Branjevo military farm primary mass grave exhumed by Professor Haglund, Dr. Haglund.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And that marking "Burial area," that was made by the provider; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct. It was not made by ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, the image has a date of 21st of September, 1995. If we can go to the next page, page 19 in the hard copy, 30 in e-court. We're now looking at an image with the date of 27 September 1995, and if you can describe what we're looking at now.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's the same area and you can see more clearly the farm buildings. In the area, if you follow the tracks around, you'll find the tracks are more defined in this image, and from my examination of these images, I believe that the -- the title there indicates that -- that there was a disturbance of that mass graves, that the mass graves has been opened and is in the process of being robbed, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And again, those white markings are the conclusion of the provider?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, they are, and I -- I don't -- I don't see a backhoe or front loader on that image. I see them marked that way. What we used -- what I used this image for was locating the area of the mass graves and the execution point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we go to image 71 now, 86 in e-court. Is there anything significant about what we're looking at here? Or can you tell us what area this is in?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is, if you like, the before photograph of Cancari Road 12 secondary mass graves. You can see a line that crosses from the top left to the middle right. Next to that is where the mass graves will be created. But you can see on the 7th of September, 1995, that that grave has not yet been created.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page. And this is an image dated 27 September 1995, the same date as the image of Branjevo military farm. And if you can describe what we're looking at here, and perhaps the usher can assist you and you can mark on this image the significant features.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: One significant point is that in these images you would invariably see the tracks of vehicles, and if you follow that line and that line, you can see what are the tracks of vehicles. And when we examined the mass graves, we would find those tracks embedded in the soil. I'm not saying those specific tracks, but we would find tracks which matched imagery. And if you look at this area, you see what looks to be an open pit, which is exactly where Cancari Road 12 secondary grave is located, and it looks to be open and not yet covered up or not yet filled with bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If you can put a CR12 within that rectangle. There's fine.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And then initial and date it.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be separately admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4511, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And if we can go to the next page, 73 in the hard copy and 88 in e-court. We're now looking at an image dated the 2nd of October, 1995. If you can describe what we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that you can clearly see that the mass grave has now been filled in, and you can see the vehicle tracks. You can recognise the vehicle tracks from the previous image around the mass graves, and it shows vehicle tracks from a heavy machine which has levelled the mass graves, and you can see those tracks radiating out from the mass graves area. So this is effectively an image after the grave has been filled with bodies and covered up, and then we would use this image to identify that site and then we would uncover that mass graves and exhume the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And this particular grave, Cancari Road 12, was exhumed by Professor Richard Wright in 1998; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In 1998, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And can you just remind us what was found in Cancari Road 12? Like, were there human remains located there?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were. I was present at the mortuary when those bodies were examined, and I examined artefacts from those bodies. There were a number of complete and partial human remains located within that secondary mass graves. There were items of identification and items which provided a strong link to Srebrenica and July of 1995, and documents which identified persons missing from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender that book in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4512, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that we took the first break earlier, the Chamber is minded to take the second break at 10 past 5.00 for 25 minutes. So could you start, Mr. Karadzic, now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Excellencies. Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, too, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since there is page 19 that's still fresh in our minds, I'd like us to go back to it so you can mark something on it. I believe it's 23633, although I don't know the page number in e-court. We saw it a moment ago. It has just been admitted. It received a new P number, whereas the old 65 ter number is 23633, page 19 in the photo album.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I think it's page 30 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the number of that marked version? It's probably P4510. This one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have it enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, you say that you know where the people were buried and where the execution took place. Can you mark the spot of execution.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I've marked the area in red.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the burial?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's the square at the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned and are familiar with the testimony of Drazen Erdemovic. Do you know that he corrected his testimony recently in this courtroom and he said that he arrived at Branjevo at 11.00 and that at that point in time there were neither prisoners more graves there? Were you shown his testimony by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure he corrected the evidence as to be specific as the time when he arrived. But what is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, he and another witness marked another spot at place of execution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was referring to the time you referred to, but please be specific in putting questions. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, at page 25374 of the transcript, he did say that he arrived at approximately 11.00, although he was not certain of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a bit different connotation. He said -- what Mr. Karadzic said, he corrected his testimony recently and he arrived at Branjevo at 11.00. But -- but I'm not sure if you need to put in all those things. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic? Would you like to keep this image for now? Shall we ask the witness to initial and date this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not just yet, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were, however, informed, and you mentioned that in the forensic summary of 2000, on page 9, that Erdemovic had said that the executions took place approximately between 10.00 and 3.00 and that some 1.200 people were killed. Now we see that he arrived at 11.00. How many sets of mortal remains were found in this location?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would have to check the reports specifically, because (a) I can't remember and I want it to be correct, but also the number of victims is much more accurately described by DNA results because there were body parts in that grave and I would be able to check my report from 2000, 2001, but that figure has since changed because of the DNA analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree or did you learn that before the alleged executions no grave was dug out?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I -- I think I understand the question. Prior to July of 1995, the aerial imagery shows that there was no grave in that area, and following the exhumation of that grave, we located -- or, the ICTY located a mass grave in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Manning, do you have any experience from some other civil wars, and, if so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No. I was not involved in investigations of war crimes until I came to the Tribunal and began working on the Srebrenica case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will put to you what Erdemovic testified to as one of the alleged perpetrators. He said that between 11.00 and 2.00 or 3.00, taking out ten people from the buses at a time and taking them some 200 metres away, executing them and returning for the next group of ten, they killed 1.200 people within that limited period. Can you imagine that scene, and can you imagine that heap of victims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure you have a -- yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree that Mr. Erdemovic said 11.00, but I'd like a citation for the 2.00 or 3.00, because my recollection was he said 3.00 or 4.00. So if Mr. Karadzic is going to put this scenario, then it needs to be factually accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, yes. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In certain statements he mentioned between 2.00 and 3.00, whereas in others between 3.00 and 4.00, but it may be as Mr. Mitchell wants it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You need to be precise, but I don't see the point of putting all those things, but please proceed. Be precise if you'd like to put -- give reference to Mr. Erdemovic's or others' evidence to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my wish for the witness to say whether he took Mr. Erdemovic's words for granted and whether he can accept that during that period 1.200 people were killed, ten at a time, and whether there were 1.200 people who were found in this particular mass grave or related to that mass grave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, whilst I've heard Mr. Erdemovic's testimony and read it on a number of occasions, my job as an investigator is to corroborate or disprove such statements. That was the process that we undertook for the exhumation/autopsy process. The mass grave at Branjevo military farm had been robbed of a significant number of bodies, yet there was still a significant number of bodies located there. Again, I don't want to give the figure because I don't want to get it wrong, but it was in excess of a hundred bodies, and I can well imagine 1.200 men and boys executed at Branjevo military farm and I can base that on the examination of the grave site and the examination of the numbers of bodies and body parts in the secondary mass graves. Whether it was 1.000 or 1.200, I can accept easily that it was a significant execution point, that the mass grave was full of bodies and that those bodies were then robbed and taken to a significant number of primary -- of secondary mass graves along Cancari Road 12, 11, 10, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you, Mr. Manning. However, in the Krstic case, on page 3618 of the 26th of May, 2000, you said that the OTP dispatched investigators to the location pointed out by Erdemovic and that: [In English] "... approximately 500 hundred Muslims had been executed at that location on 16th of July, 1995."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the English part. It was -- when you change into English, please put a pause, significant pause, so that we wouldn't miss any part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So I'll read out quoting directly from the English version.
