Page 3618, the 26th of May, 2000, the Krstic case: [In English] "The Office of the Prosecutor sent the investigators to that location after Drazen Erdemovic informed Prosecution that approximately 500 Muslims had been executed at that location on the 16th of July, 1995."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, I think I missed some early part of your English. "Office of the Prosecutor sent ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "... investigators to that location after Drazen Erdemovic informed the Prosecutor that approximately 500 Muslims had been executed at that location on the 16th of July 1995."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can apologise for interrupting. The way that question is phrased is extremely misleading. The previous -- the question that Mr. Manning was asked said: This is a photograph of the Pilica Dom. At the rear of this building was the execution point examined?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We're talking about a completely different site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then let us upload that page if you'd like to pose that question. Before we upload that question, I asked you, Mr. Karadzic, whether you would like to keep this image. Would you like to keep this image for now? Yes. Why don't you initial and date this document. We can re-upload it, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we admit it as a separate Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2188, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What is your -- what is the 65 ter number for Krstic transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D5177. Page 77.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, Mr. Manning, in the forensic summary of 2007, you state that the ICMP identified 104 Srebrenica victims in this grave; correct? Page 5 of the forensic summary.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, without checking that report, I can only say I can accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. You said excess of hundred bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honours, I make the point that that is the number of bodies identified from the mass grave, not the numbers of bodies within the mass grave. That would be the end result of their examinations. Remembering that in that mass grave there were bodies parts which were very broken up and that might indicate a body part of only a foot or a leg or a hand in that grave, but that would still represent an individual in that grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We have the page in front of us, Mr. Karadzic. Is this the page you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the testimony, and I believe I've already moved on to the forensic summary of 2007, where it is stated that the ICMP identified 104 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why, Mr. Manning, in your view, out of the alleged 1.200 they were unable to identify more than 104?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Karadzic asked if I could well imagine that many number. I can, but the primary mass grave at Branjevo military farm was robbed. The bodies were removed, and the process of identifying the human remains is, I assume, still continuing. Therefore, that there were at least 100 victims identified from that primary mass grave indicates to me that the significant number of bodies removed from that mass grave have either been identified in Cancari Road or some other mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you establish the number involved? Did anyone establish the number of victims at the Branjevo Farm, and did you accept that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That figure would be most accurate from Mr. Janc's report in that the definitive number of victims from that grave and that execution would be the number identified from the Branjevo military farm primary mass grave and the number of victims identified in the related secondary mass graves along Cancari Road. So if you took their most recent figures, added up four or five or however many secondary graves with the primary grave, you would have an accurate count of the number of identified bodies so far from that execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, do you know that in that area the war went on for some 45 months? Did you know that a differentiation should be made between those who lost their lives during those 45 months from those who were killed in the fighting in July, and finally, those who were unlawfully killed had to be identified, those who were not killed in combat? Did anyone draw your attention to that, that there were different times involved as far as deaths were concerned and burials as well?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm aware that the conflict extended for some particular time. I don't believe there was conflict in the area of Branjevo military farm, but I have absolutely no evidence to indicate that bodies other than those killed following the fall of Srebrenica executed at the Branjevo military farm were placed in the Branjevo military farm mass grave and then removed to secondary graves. Part of the work that we undertook, that the experts undertook, was to identify that the grave we were examining was (a) connected to Srebrenica, and (b) showed no evidence of being an amalgam of other graves or a grave that was used over years. There was no evidence of that in the graves that we examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the statements of Drazen Erdemovic, did you find the following information: that on that day the guards had informed him that there had been burials there beforehand as well? So it's the plural, "burials."

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that evidence from Mr. Erdemovic or any other person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Erdemovic confirmed that here as well in this courtroom, that he had been informed about that, that the guard had told him that there had been burials there earlier on as well. All right. Now I'm going to ask you something else, Mr. Manning. Do you know what the situation was like in Srebrenica during those three and a half years? Do we agree that there was no public transportation there? Do we agree that banks were not operating there?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I only know of the circumstances in Srebrenica from speaking to witnesses and examining video and photographic records. I know that it was particularly difficult, that there were some records of near starvation, and I completely accept that the normal functions of government would have been either non-existent or barely operating and delivered by the UN in -- in some measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point you said, and I can find that if you don't confirm it for me now, that many things complicated the investigation there. Can you enumerate that for us? What were the things that made your work more complicated -- or, rather, establishing the truth in the Srebrenica case?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The sheer volume of the executions made it a long-term investigation. Perhaps you're referring to the fact that the primary graves were disturbed. Had we simply examined non-robbed, non-disturbed primary graves, we would have had intact bodies, and we would have been able to (a) count them, and (b) probably identify them much more quickly. In trying to hide the graves, the robbing of the graves broke up the bodies, tore the bodies apart and made not only the identification of those people very difficult but significantly increased the number of crime scenes that we had to examine. Had the primary mass graves not been touched, we probably could have exhumed them in a short time of a year or two and worked on the findings from those exhumations and autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Apart from that, was everything in order? Did you know that experts had serious objections to the correctness and regularity of the investigations there, and even Haglund himself called the 1996 investigations a three-ring circus? Also, there were serious objections with respect to Haglund's work, too.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm aware of the allegations against Dr. Haglund. They were dealt with prior to my arrival at the ICTY, and I wasn't part of those issues, but in no way did I see any significant irregularities, any significant criticism of the work that flowed from Dr. Haglund's reports to the Chambers and from the other experts, Professor Wright, Mr. Baraybar, Dr. Clark, et cetera. I don't have first-hand knowledge of the issues that Dr. Haglund faced, but I don't believe that there was dissent thereafter in relation to the exhumation/autopsy process and how it was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For the participants, Mr. Haglund, in the Popovic case, on pages 19065 through -068, said that these investigations from 1996 were a three-ring circus. Do you know, Mr. Manning, that Dr. Snow, who is a highly prominent forensic anthropologist of world renown, said that these things done in 1996 were "sloppy science"?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I don't recall that specific quote. I was aware of, broadly, the allegations concerning Dr. Haglund. They'd been dealt with before I attended the Tribunal, and I didn't examine them thereafter, so I can't comment on that particular comment except to say that I didn't see evidence of that in my examination of the documents produced by Dr. Haglund and his team, acknowledging that I'm not a forensic expert or an anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I see the time Excellency. Should I go on or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break for --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can I just raise two small points in less than a minute. The first point is the Prosecution does not oppose the Defence request to have assistance of defence expert in courtroom for Butler testimony, and the second point is I just want to remind everyone that Mr. Djurdjevic also has to finish tomorrow, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My information -- that he could remain with us a bit in the morning -- on the morning of Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But that's changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. Tomorrow is Wednesday. I just wanted to mention, because we only spoke today about Mr. Manning to have to conclude tomorrow, but Mr. Djurdjevic as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But he has to return then, if we cannot finish him tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We'll take a break for 25 minutes and resume at 20 to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, while the logistical concerns should not affect the proper time for cross-examination, we will do our utmost to accommodate the situations of the witnesses. For today, if necessary, we'll extend our sitting until up to 7.20 or 7.30, depending on the situation, and tomorrow we decided to sit in an extended format, i.e., 9.00 to 3.00. Then I will hope that that could solve the situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence will respond to all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, please do not feel attacked at any point in time. I'm not attacking you or anyone else. I would just like us to do away with all this confusion. And now I'm going to put to you what my thesis is. My thesis is that this was a theatre of war for almost 45 months. People lost their lives there, and these people were buried -- I mean, you would bury those who belonged to the other side in mass graves, whereas you'd bury your own in family graves. Were you informed about these deaths there and that people who lost their lives in combat were buried in mass graves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry for interrupting immediately, but first I'd like to clarify "the people lost their lives there," and secondly, Mr. Karadzic was given a chance to cross-examine Erdemovic last week and this was never the case that was put to him, and I think it's inappropriate for now. We tried to push Mr. Karadzic on what his specific case was last week and he wouldn't put a case to Mr. Erdemovic, and to now suggest that the bodies in any of these graves or particularly at Branjevo Farm are combat I think is inappropriate when he didn't put it to that particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic, you heard Mr. Mitchell's intervention. Yes. Please reformulate in a more precise manner or put one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Excellency, may I just respond? Last time I did not want to admit something that Mr. Mitchell wanted to get from me. What he has to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed. Put one question at a time to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Mitchell, did you know that people lost their lives during those 45 months and that the victims of the other side were buried by their adversaries in mass graves through so-called sanitisation procedures?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're now referring to the specific Branjevo Farm, do you -- are you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. This entire area that Mr. Manning dealt with, this entire war zone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I accept that many people were killed and burials took place, no doubt some mass burials. We saw no evidence that the Srebrenica graves contained bodies from a previous era. We saw no specific evidence that the bodies in the mass graves were not executed and buried within those mass graves which were hidden. They were not, in my view, "asanacija" or a cleansing of the -- of the battleground. They were clandestinely dug primary mass graves which held the bodies of, in many cases, victims who were bound or blindfolded or both and shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will get to that, Mr. Manning. Tell us now, please, did you ever see executions carried out by shrapnel and were there any victims here that had been killed by shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: There was evidence from the chief archaeologist Dr. Wright and from the anthropologist Chris Lawrence and also Dr. Clark at that some bodies, particularly from Glogova 1 and 2, Ravnice, and Zeleni Jadar graves bore shrapnel injury, that they had charring and they were burnt and that the bodies had been disfigured by explosion, and there was some evidence clearly of explosions at Pilica Dom and Kravica warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at this, Mr. Manning. You said that in addition to Muslim ritual objects, you did not find any of another provenance. For example, you didn't find any Christian objects. Were there any Christians in these graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I didn't -- sorry, the whole team did not find specific evidence of any other religion except Islam within the artefacts located on the bodies and within the graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to show you one of these -- that is 2478, 65 ter. So I'd like to show you an example of a Serb buried there. Can you explain that? How else would a Serb be in a mass graves except by way of "asanacija," sanitisation of the terrain? Do you have any explanation? How would a Serb get there? How would a Serb get into a mass grave unless it was a question of sanitisation, not being recognised by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I believed you were going to show me something, but I don't know of any Serb victim who was confirmed to be in a Srebrenica mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we take a look at Lazete 1, page 17. 523. Please take a look at that. 523, Nusret Zimic with a traffic licence for a particular vehicle, and then there's another one, 523, Gojko Polic. That's what it says. Obviously they did not recognise him and they buried him during the sanitisation of the terrain. Do you have any information about that? Do you know how come a Serb was part of this execution, if there was one, and how come there was a Serb in a Srebrenica unit?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document Mr. Karadzic is --

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just a second. We can collapse B/C/S. That's the second item in the number Lazete 1, 523, ID document, something, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is one that I produced, and what it shows is that on the body, Lazete 1, 523, there was found an identification document titled "Registration number," and the name on that document was Polic, Gojko. That doesn't indicate that that individual was in the grave. It indicates that document was in the grave in the possession of a victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how would the victim have that if it were a Tuzla licence or registration?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Well, firstly, I don't know why that person would have that identification document, but I need to correct myself. Without checking the complete number, in those -- in that time, the numbering system was somewhat different so that item 523 might have been a document loose in the grave rather than on a body. In later instances, I would know from the number. We would need to check that, but this indicates to me that that document was found in the Lazete 2 mass grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What does that the highlight or emboldened characters mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why are some of the entries emboldened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't actually know, and I'm not quite sure if that's an artefact of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you show the upper part of it. Is that, "The highlighted entries indicate names located in part or whole in the ICRC list of missing from Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I do recall now. So the emboldened is entries that are located in the ICRC missing list; that is, an individual listed as missing from Srebrenica or the closest match to that name that we could find.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, could you please take a look at this, line 3, Lenjinac Husein. He has a cheque-book and a personal ID. Over those three years, had a bank been working in Srebrenica and could people pay by using cheques?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I don't know, but I suspect not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You thank you. Please take a look at 514. Again this is a bank receipt.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at 567. It is a health insurance card, and health insurance did not function. Everything had to be paid for. In Srebrenica there was no health insurance.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- I think Mr. Karadzic is referring to 582, and I accept that. If I may, I've examined these documents and seen that some of the documents relate to periods well preceding the fall of Srebrenica. Some documents went back clearly to the individual's grandfather or family, and I assume that this individual who was born in -- I'm sorry, I notice that there are very old individuals within the grave, and I recall some of the documentation was 10 and 20, and 30 and 40 years old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Item 567 also has health insurance card, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at 634, please, identification card from Rogatica. A man from Rogatica participated in the fighting. He was killed and buried when the terrain was being cleared. Do you have any proof that things were different, because people from Rogatica didn't flee to Srebrenica. The fate of Rogatica was different.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't comment on -- I can't comment on -- on that only to say that that individual was located within a mass grave which we clearly identified to be connected to the fall of Srebrenica and which contained the bodies of victims who were bound and, in some cases, blindfolded and executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Manning, do you know that POWs couldn't hold on to their passports? Have a look at the last entry on this page. It refers to passport 641. I think the layout I have is somewhat different. Have a look at 641, passport number 2511 -- it's the eighth entry from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I see that entry and I've examined those items. The majority of the bodies we found in the graves had some form of identification, normally wallets. That was a very common instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Above that entry there is someone with an ID card and a military ID. The number is 637; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't have to have a look at the next page. I'm already looking at the following page. Just a moment, please. 648, for example, a medical report. Let's see the date. Who is the doctor who drafted this? Have these documents been kept?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I can't answer that. That's something that the ICTY could answer. In -- in the Lazete grave, many of those documents were handed over to PHR, Physicians for Human Rights, and they worked very heavily on trying to identify the victims, but you would have to ask the ICTY if they still hold that item. There is a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You confirmed that you found Dutch newspapers dated April 1995 on one of the victims; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct. We found a number of items connected to the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us why would someone have a Dutch newspaper on him or herself for three and a half months and take this newspaper with him or her if that person was captured into captivity? What sort of an explanation could you provide for this? What is the logic?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, to my knowledge some of those newspapers were cut into small squares. We assumed that they were used as cigarette paper, and the photographs of those items would show you that they were small pieces of newsprint. As to why they kept them, I can't answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you did not say that these were cut-outs. You said that there was a Dutch newspaper that was found. The date on the newspaper was April. You saw the date. You saw the month. So it was a whole newspaper; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, that's not correct, although that's not to say that there was not a complete page among the tens of thousands of artefacts. But I specifically recall a Dutch newspaper cut in, what I assumed, to be cigarette-paper size.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we please see page 19. Just a minute. The matter is a religious one. No. It's lower down. 471. Silver engraved -- a silver cigarette box. You also came across silver pocket watches, and so on and so forth; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's have a look at what you put under the column "Religious Artefacts." You have prayer beads and then there is a triangular cotton bag. Do you know what the purpose of that bag is? Did your hosts in Bosnia inform you of the customs of war in our country?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For example, did they tell you what a Muslim fighter, what a Serbian fighter, would have on themselves, what they would do, what sort of customs they had, amulets, religious inscriptions, other sort of ribbons? Did anybody tell you about such things? Takbirs?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm not sure I discussed it at length, but I did some research as to what the items we located within the grave were. I found out what a muska was and that these items of small copies of the Koran or small paragraphs from the Koran were routinely carried by people of the Muslim faith, and I saw those sort of documents and pieces of material within the mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now on the next page we have prayer beads. That's clear, although you find prayer beads in almost all religions; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. I would accept that, to my knowledge, Christian and Muslim religious people have prayer beads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us have a look at the following: There are these pouches or -- do you know that these things are used to keep ritual objects, religious inscriptions, religious artefacts, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. And where we could identify what the text was or the artefact was, we would indicate it. And as I said, the only religion that we could confirm was Islam.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have a look at the following page. I'm not sure it's the same one. Is that page 12? We saw the reference to the Koran. You confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What page is this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The previous page, if you are referring to "Miniature Koran in red plastic box." Previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and we went back to the previous page. Could we see page 20 now. Could we see the following page. Could we see the following page, please. Could I see the number, please, the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have B/C/S version, Mr. Karadzic, in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you upload both then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 20 in the Serbian version now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Lazete 2C.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at it. 471, a pocket watch, was found, a silver pocket watch on a chain; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can see the B/C/S version, but I remember from the English version, yes, and it was engraved "Tunnel Krizevci 5/3/1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Krizevci, yes. It's page 19 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The page we were looking at just before, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please see the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look at this. The following page in the Serbian, please. That's it in the Serbian version. Have a look at how many passports there were with these people. There were driving licenses, a number of letters, and at least three passports, a bank receipt, a bank document from the Sarajevo agricultural -- the Sarajevo Economic Bank and so on and so forth. Mr. Manning, did you know that a POW couldn't have a passport on himself and that the detainees in the detention unit here similarly don't have their passports on them?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I would accept that. However, our investigation, witness statements, the exhumations work, indicated that these individuals had been captured and executed in possession of those documents. I don't know why they were not removed. There was a consistency in all the graves that the majority of the victims had some identification material with them or some personal, small personal effects. I believe that Nova Kasaba 99 was the only grave in which we found significant belongings, some bags, but the majority of them had what they had on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that accusations were levelled against Serbian policemen or troops or individuals, according to which after people were captured they would take the passports and other valuables from these captives? So how can we reconcile these two claims? How can we reconcile this claim with the fact that people had, well, both passports and valuables on them?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I give an example from Kravica warehouse. The survivor who may have given evidence to the Chamber indicated he was captured or gave himself up. He was held on Sandici meadow. He was then taken the approximate kilometre to Kravica warehouse where the execution took place. He didn't indicate, from my recollection, that he was thoroughly searched. Other accounts from survivors indicate the same thing. And I do accept that accounts during the war indicate that prisoners and others would have material removed from them. In this instance, the bodies were found with their identification documents and minor artefacts in their possession in the majority of cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, Mr. Manning, let me ask you whether you agree with the following: Did you find out that up -- that the killing in Kravica took place after an incident? Goods or items weren't listed or taken. The detainees were kept, and after the incident these people were killed. Were you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm aware that the men were taken to the warehouse and detained there and they were executed there en masse, and I'm aware, although I wasn't part of that investigation, of an individual who had - and I'm trying to remember - either tried to grab a weapon or taken a weapon or attempted to take a weapon and that's when the executions commenced, but I wasn't involved in that part of the investigation. It was after I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For your information, he was killed although he went to light up a cigarette. They weren't treated as POWs, Mr. Manning. They were being kept, and this is how had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, do you know that Islamic fighters, even our Serbian fighters, wear ribbons, ritual ribbons, around their heads, and the Muslims have ribbons on which you have the Tegbir inscription from the Koran or their mother's embroider their ribbons. These ribbons are called mother's halal, and they are used by these soldiers when they go to war. Were you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you about this. Did the hosts, the local people provide you with information on everything over there? Please have a look at how these ribbons were used, these ribbons that were sometimes used as blindfolds. Sometimes you refer to them as ribbons that might be used as blindfolds. Have a look at what they look like. The fourth and the fifth from the bottom with the serrated edge, and then it says another one with a serrated edge. 394, pink cotton ribbon, and a blue ribbon for hats. Can you imagine anyone who wants to shoot people and then prepares all these ribbons that he could blindfold the person without tying up that person's hands?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the items that Mr. Karadzic is referring to, I examined each and every one of them. I believe that the items represented here are blindfolds. In no way was there evidence that any of those items were (a) marked with any Islamic text, or (b) produced as a scarf or a ribbon. The majority of the items were scrap cloth, particularly looking as if they had been used in a process, an industrial process, perhaps covering furniture, perhaps items of clothing. They were scraps of cloth, and they were tied in many, many instances around the head of the individuals. I did not see anything that would indicate to me or to the experts who examined the blindfolds that they were in any way (a) a religious item, and (b) used as a headscarf or covering. They were scraps of cloth which were not, what I would consider, being produced by mothers for their sons. They were also tied, in the instances that I saw, very strongly around the head of the individuals, and in a significant number of the items I found what I believed to be human hair, clumps of hair, caught in the knot. And I also would refer to testimony of survivors, for instance, from Orahovac, who indicated that they were blindfolded, and also I believe from memory at the dam at Petkovci. But certainly in Orahovac, and I'm not sure if the Chamber has heard from that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Whose hair would be tied up with a ribbon used by a combatant?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In the instances that I saw, I saw bodies in some of the graves which still had some of their hair on their skulls, and you could see that that hair was caught up in the knot of the blindfold. And I'm not an expert on human hair, but when I examined the blindfolds, I saw what I believe to be human hair within the knots and I'm assuming that that's the human hair from the head which that blindfold was on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that there were satin and velvet ribbons, these ribbons of very expensive material? Dr. Christopher Lawrence confirmed here before this Court that the material used was fairly expensive. Did you have any such information?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just get a cite for that. I don't recall Mr. Lawrence giving that evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you don't remember, we'll find it, but I'm familiar with this case, and I'm sure you're familiar with it better than I am. He said that. He confirmed that it was rather expensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that there was shiny material that was used, satin and velvet?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't remember velvet, and I wouldn't say the material was satin. One of the experts described the material as having a sheen, that being somewhat shiny, and I accept that, but as I said before, that material that could be referred to as shiny was in -- in such a distinct pattern that you could see it had been cut from a -- from a square of cloth, and the inside of that cloth had been used for something else, and the scalloping around the edge of the cloth indicated that the middle of the square of cloth had been cut out. So this material, whether it be shiny or expensive was an off-cut from another process. It was scrap material in many cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the entry 470, which is entry number 8 from the bottom. It says, "Pink satin-like material - patterned." And in many cases the edges were scalloped or serrated. Do you know what this means when you say it was scalloped or serrated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer. Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be fair. Dr. Lawrence did say -- he was asked about a particular piece of fabric [overlapping speakers] expensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He answered yes somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct. At transcript 22474.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I located it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The scalloped edges was the pattern and how it was described. It was roughly cut. It wasn't sewn. And I liken it, if you take a handkerchief and place it over a glass tightly held, if you cut a line around the glass, the remaining material that you have would have an irregular scalloped pattern where the material was bunched up, and that's what we saw in those scalloped-edge pieces of material, and they were not embroidered finished, they were off -cuts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's go through these things here and see what it says. Have a look at 470. Does it say pink satin-like material with a pattern?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there embroidered material? I don't know how this is going to be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Some of the blindfolds had an embroidered flour pattern in them. It was a small three- or four-lobed flower which had been sewn by machine into the material, and I think it had holes in the flower. And that was repeated across the material. And again, those -- the majority of those strips of cloth appeared to be the off-cut of a process, that they were the bits left behind when something else was produced, the scrap material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you establish that? After that much time being in the country itself, how were you able to establish that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: If you examine the blindfolds, and there are photographs within my report and in other reports, when the blindfolds were examined at the mortuary, they would be cleaned, photographed, and in some instances the blindfolds would be pulled out in the shape of a square and you could see that they were clearly the leftover from some process. We examined the blindfolds, the cloth, and Dr. Maljaars examined them, and there are photographs that show the blindfold in that state, in that frame with the inside missing, in many instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, did you know that a warrior carries the presence of a female, be it a mother or sister? Let's look at 23632, 65 ter, photograph number 4. Did you know that people carried something with them like a mother's halal? If your mother presented you with one, if you were killed in combat, you go straight to heaven. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No, not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at photograph number 4 from 65 ter 23632. Volume 2. Volume number 2. The ERN number is 0705-2817. Page 9 in e-court. Have a look at this. Are you trying to say that a Serb soldier would have a scarf like this in his equipment and used it when necessary?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that that was a blindfold, and it was put on the victim's head prior to execution. This was one of the pieces of cloth that we found and identified as a blindfold, or it could be a ligature, if I look at the number, but I believe it's a blindfold.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the culture of Serbs and Muslims and the way they live? If so, would you ascribe this particular colour and design to Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I don't see anything that would indicate a religious affinity in that piece of cloth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what colours are sported by Serb women as opposed to Muslim women, and how would you explain a Serb soldier having something like this at hand?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the colours sported by Serb women as opposed to Muslim women, and I'm not aware that this blindfold was carried by a Serb soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have a look at photograph 61, which is at page 64 in e-court in hard copy. Page 64, photograph 61. The ERN number is 2874. Did you see some fighters, including Serb fighters, wearing scarves or bands around their heads on any photographs or footage?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: If we're talking about the conflict if Bosnia, yes, and I believe some of the members of the Serb forces who entered Srebrenica had headscarves. I think black. This individual in the image is from the Lazete -- Lazete 2 mass grave and is a blindfold on his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a soldier, Mr. Manning, and what is on his chest and around his waist?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I don't know if he's a soldier. I assume he's of military age. He may very well have been a soldier. Without checking the autopsy reports, I can't say specifically. It looks like clothing. It looks like trousers. If it was military clothing or equipment, it would be noted on the autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at page 91? Sorry, page 94, photograph 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for it, could you explain how Serb soldiers had these objects on them, the ones that you termed blindfolds? Page 94, yes. If you were familiar with our customs, would you ascribe this item to a Serb or a Muslim; in other words, if that person was given it by a Serb woman or a Muslim woman?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I can't answer that question other than to say that that item was found in a mass grave. I believe it to be a blindfold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your question was whether witness could explain how Serb soldiers had these objects on them, the ones you term blindfolds like this. Is it your case that Serb soldiers always carried with them the object that can be used, properly used, as blindfolds? Not in this colour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assert, Your Excellency, that they never did. It was not common to Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, can you tell us how come one of these alleged blindfolds was found in the pocket of a victim?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. I can assume, and there is some evidence from the survivors that they took their blindfolds off, and I assume that that's what happened, but I can't -- and without a specific reference, I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to find it? Do you remember specifying that a blindfold was found in a person's pocket?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I can accept that -- I don't recall that, but I can accept that. And as I say, I can only assume why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I told you that religious objects were not to be shown to nonbelievers or stepped on, would you see it as something familiar? Does it ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I currently work within the Middle East. I'm familiar with the people of the region, particularly the Islamic people. In some cases that religious imperative may be applied. In my time in Bosnia I did not find -- and I do not mean to be disrespectful, I did not find the Bosnian Muslims to be particularly religious or to be particularly ardent about such things, but I'm not an expert on Bosnian Muslim religious practices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, just for -- purely for planning purpose, I'd like to inquire of you how much more time do you need to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd need another hour, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In that case, we will take a break for five minutes and resume 10 to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the remainder of this session, we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Yes. Mr. Karadzic, we'll sit up to, if necessary, 7.20 or 7.30, but I expect you to conclude before then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Excellency. Can we have page 103.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll show you just one more. Page 103. Photograph number 100. Zoom in, please. Can you see the jagged edge and the pattern? Could you provide any other explanation other than this being a religious item? We can zoom in. You can see that it has a clear pattern. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is what I've been discussing. A great majority of the blindfolds were exactly the same as this material in different colours, and I've always assumed that they came from the same source, that they're scrap material. And, Mr. Karadzic, the scalloping on the edges of the blindfold are quite clear. You can see that they are cut edges. They haven't been embroidered. They haven't been end-stitched. If you would have spread this blindfold out, you would see that it formed the outside of a square piece of cloth, and the material in the middle of that cloth has been cut away. And if you found that material, you'd find that the scalloped edges matched and this is a piece of cloth that was repeated in this form across many of the graves in startling similarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how do you know that, Mr. Manning, and is what you are saying the only explanation? Are other explanations possible?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I have physically examined each and every one of these items. I've seen the shape that -- that if you were to spread that blindfold out, you would see the same shape that you see in Dr. Maljaars' report and the photographs that I produced. It is clearly an off-cut of some other process, but what's more striking is that many, many, many other blindfolds were exactly the same construction, and they were tied around the heads of individuals who had been executed. In some instances the same material was used as a ligature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. Are you trying to say, Mr. Manning, that these extensions, these tassels of sorts, are not identical and at equal distances and that they were created randomly?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That they are identical and equidistant or not?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No. As I said before, they are off-cuts, and those scalloped edges are irregular, and it is my belief and I've produced exactly the same pattern that the material was bunched together, it was cut off, and that's the scrap that's left. It is not embroidered. It is not equidistant. They are not tassels. It is not in any way, in my view, a religious artefact. And, in fact, this particular type of blindfold was in pink, blue, and I can't recall the third colour. It certainly wasn't Islamic green, and none of the blindfolds or cloth ligatures that I saw had any Islamic writing references or material on them whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, if you were in the Middle East, would you be able to notice that Christians and Jews there prefer darker colours and monochromatic clothing, whereas Muslims, and especially Muslim women, choose coloured patterns and lighter colours?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think I can speak particularly well on that matter. The Arab women that I know of in the region predominantly wear black -- black abayas. Some of the men wear white. Some of the men where colours. Some of them have different headdresses. They are like all of us, different people and different clothing requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that you found the so-called blindfolds which did not have a knot; that is to say, that were in a single piece?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Some of the blindfolds had been broken up, had been damaged. If I could not establish that there was a blindfold, i.e., it was the same shape as the head, it was a round circle of cloth bound in a knot, I would not accept it as a blindfold. And the photos you see of -- of blindfolds which have been spread out like this were in our examination of them at the mortuary, that they were cleaned, photographed, and spread out, the knot removed, to -- to show that, in this case, the similarity with other cloths.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have look at 65 ter 2478, although it does have a P number. I won't dwell on this any longer. I won't show any more photographs since I have no time. Page 24 in hard copy. In the English version it may be different, but -- well, 24 in the Serbian, and we'll manage with the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The top of the page, 596. A band, a cloth band, without a knot, pale in colour. How come it was without a knot?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Two pages ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, accepting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It says, "Discoloured strip of cloth - minus knot." Bottom of the page probably. That may be it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 596, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it sewn or is it this circle? You said you used to find these circles made of cloth.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would probably need to check the autopsy report and the photograph, but I note that I've indicated that it is on the head of the individual and it may be that the knot has fallen away and is in the body bag. It may be that the knot has simply rotted away, but I indicated on these documents where the blindfold or ligature was found. In this instance, I've said it was on the person's head. Clearly there's a photograph and a record of that appearing as a blindfold. And if you look further up that column, you see that I've indicated item 580 was located within the grave. So in this instance we have a blindfold which doesn't have a knot, one of the many hundreds, that is on someone's head. But, again, if I could see the photograph of the item or the autopsy report that would help me recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have the next page in English, please, and please take a look at this. Look at all the kinds of bandannas you can find here without a knot, embroidered with floral embroidery, and a few are green. A few are green, Mr. Manning. There are some made of satin. Please look at your very own paper here. How did you rule this out? How did you rule out something that you had not even been informed about, namely this possibility that these were gifts from women and ritual artefacts? How could a Serb soldier have this many embroidered cloths?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, my -- my view is that the blindfolds and cloth ligatures that were the same, which matched, appeared to come from a manufacturing process. I don't know, and I assume that if I had an intention to blindfold a significant number of people, I would go to a clothing factory, and I would grab a great handful of cloths and I would use those as blindfolds. And I note some of the items that I've listed there were used opportunistically, a piece of handkerchief, a piece of clothing, a piece of pants. And I've indicated on this document the condition of those items and, more importantly, where they were located. If I've identified the item as a blindfold, it is because there is a photograph of an item on a body and an autopsy report that indicates that, or the blindfold is located within the grave and is in such -- and is documented, and is of such similar construction and shape and has human hair in the knot that it was considered to be a blindfold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, the LZ01-596, the discoloured strip of cloth minus the knot, we do actually have a photograph of it here on the -- it's on that large composite. So if there's any further questions on it, we can actually bring that up and the witness can look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to see the picture, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It might be better to give the witness the hard copy. The one in e-court isn't particularly good resolution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we not -- yes. We don't have any difficulty giving the hard copy to the witness. But why don't we upload it at the same time. What's the e-court number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, it was Exhibit 4508. It's in the far right-hand column, and it's the seventh photo down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I just need the reference to the body number again, LZ-2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The image has an arrow on it indicating the blindfold in situ on the individual's head; that is, placed on the individual's head. We could check the autopsy report, but normally that arrow would indicate a bullet hole corresponding through the skull with a hole through the blindfold. In this instance, you can see the blindfold adhering to the victim's head, covering his eyes. If you -- if you see it's where the cursor is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the one, Your Honour. I believe -- you can see that this is an image at the mortuary. The white underneath the body is a body bag. These photos were take when the body first arrived at the mortuary, before the body was cleaned up, but the pathologist would look at that body and examine that blindfold and report on that blindfold when he or she examined the body, noting the blindfold and the injuries to the skull.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please indicate which one that is, and where does it say 956? Can we identify that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is no arrow there, the one that you referred to. And let us see whether that is a ribbon that is not tied but is braided or sewn.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I've circled the arrow on that photograph, and without examining the cleaned-up version of that blindfold, I can't tell you the construction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is one of the ones. Lazete 1 is in Mr. Manning's second or third report. These images of LZ1 are not contained in those -- in the two volumes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary, you can find the original picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes. We can find the original and then maybe tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or disclose it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Defence should have it by --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: They should already have it but we can find it and offer it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Could you initial and date it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2189, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us now deal with what was done here. You said today at one point in time that the Prosecutor -- rather, the investigation from the OTP agreed with the findings. What about the Defence, the Serb side, as a party concerned? Did they agree to anything, and did they take any part in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: If -- if I understand the last part of your question, the exhumation and autopsy process was conducted by predominantly the ICTY. We very deliberately excluded nationals from any of the entities being involved in that process. We had no Serbs or Muslims involved -- sorry, Bosnian Serbs or Muslims involved in that exhumation/autopsy process, and I believe that ICMP had some staff from the other entities, but Serb judicial officials or Bosnian judicial officials and investigators were excluded from the exhumation site and the autopsy examination process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After that, you or the Tribunal or the OTP, did you hand over the investigation to the Muslim side from 2001 or whatever it was that you said?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. We handed over responsibility for the mass graves to the Bosnian Commission for Missing People -- Persons, and they continued the recovery of the bodies, and the Bosnian court is conducting investigations into Srebrenica. The Office of the Prosecutor handed over investigative files.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that out there in Bosnia there is a lot of dispute involved in the work of that commission? The Serb side is challenging all of it, and the Muslim side is interested in portraying things in order to say that the number of victims is as big as possible?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm aware there's a conflict. The number of missing from Srebrenica is being defined by the independent International Commission for Missing Persons, but I'm not up-to-date on the conflict between the various entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you observed that in each and every grave the degree of degradation or decay of the bodies varied to a large degree at that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the graves showed a variance in degrees of decomposition. Perhaps less so at Orahovac 1 because of the condition of the grave, but some bodies in the same grave were completely skeletonised and others were predominantly fleshed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In one and the same grave?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, in the Kozluk mass grave, the bodies that were away from the other individuals tended to be completely skeletonised. The ones within the mass of bodies were -- tended to be fleshed. I'm not an expert, but I understand why. And we saw that in various graves. If the body was nearer to the surface, had access to oxygen or the soil conditions were such, the body would decompose differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I take that into account, that you're not an expert, but tell me, is that the only explanation?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you see, here it is experts who said that that is not the only explanation possible but that there are other explanations that are possible, too. Now I'm asking you about the blindfolds. Are your explanations the only ones, and how did you rule out all others?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: If I can, you asked me if that was the own explanation. Taking a view of the total evidence available, that's the only explanation. Had the bodies come from different time periods and different graves or had been left on the surface to decompose, there would have been evidence of that. If you took the bodies in a mass grave, some were skeletonised, some were fleshed, they were within the same grave, and there was no evidence that they had been buried in a separate incident, separated by months, years. And as to my examination of the blindfolds, every single blindfold that I identified had previously been identified by one of the experts, archaeologists and anthropologists, as a blindfold. I sought to confirm that was documented and was consistent, and if I found a blindfold that did not have a photograph showing it in situ or did not have a complete record, then would I discount that blindfold, because I took a very conservative view of only including items that we could definitively prove the process and the location of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How is it that you established that there is no proof that there were burials in stages, and did you receive any explanation to the effect as to where persons were buried over those 45 months?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm not an archaeologist. I'm not an expert. The experts that I spoke to described the graves to me. They showed me the construction of the graves. They showed me how there was evidence when a grave was disturbed, which is how they know that a primary grave was robbed. But even as a layman I could see that. If there was evidence which showed that there had been multiple burial incidents, that would be obvious in the soil, in the make-up of the grave, in the position of the bodies, in the soil and vegetation that was collected with the bodies. There would be evidence of that difference. And in some instances we found vegetation with the bodies, which is consistent with middle of summer in Bosnia, in that region. Had they been killed at a different time of year, we would expect to see evidence of that. Had they been infested by insects because they were on the surface for months, we would expect to see that. We would find that evidence. I've spoken to the experts. That's my understanding of their process, and as a layman, I saw that within the graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So now you are not conveying your own expert insight but, rather, what others said to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. He confirmed that he's not an expert, and you're still putting the questions, inviting him to tell us what he heard from experts. It's about time to conclude, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll do my best to finish fairly soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know that fighters used to put ribbons on their sleeves and elsewhere on the left and right, and do you know that the ribbons that you saw on a hand were perhaps not ligatures but a ribbon that was used to mark soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm vaguely aware that some soldiers would use that practice. I'm not aware of it being used predominantly in Bosnia. The ligatures were tightly bound around the wrists of the individuals. They were in the cloth ligatures. They were in the figure of an eight. They bound the hands of the individual, and that individual could not move their arms. I don't believe that they were armbands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we saw in those photographs of yours, Mr. Manning, we saw ribbons at different levels, if you look at the hands and arms. We can look at that, but there's not much time today. Did you see that there were remnants of a ribbon at different levels on a hand or arm?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No. We didn't find what you would describe as ribbons around the arm or the forearm or the upper arm of individuals. We found cloth ligatures binding both hands, or we found wire ligatures binding both hands, or we found a figure-eight ligature binding one hand and clearly in a shape of a figure-eight where both hands had been passed through that cloth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, the last topic and the last question, do you know people who work at ICMP, Rifet Kasetovic, Zlatan Sabanovic?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I believe Rifet Kasetovic may be someone I know. I'm not familiar with the other name, but I said before that people from Bosnia, Serbia, Croatia, are employed at ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this one, Kasetovic is the director, and Sabanovic is also a high official. What about Director Edin Jasaragic does that name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: It does not, Your Honour, but I would accept that Mr. Kasetovic was the director. It rings a memory. Probably the director of the Bosnian commission for missing people rather than the International Commission for Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't have time to ask you about the other prominent Muslims in that institution. Let me ask you this: Do you know that recently they came out with some corrections and they said that 500 were still living, and then they said that 70 were included there, although they were not victims, and then during the last week or two they came up with the following thesis: That some amputees were include among the dead for no reason whatsoever. There was no justification for that. These people are still living. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Manning. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have about three objections to that. One, it's assuming a lot of things that aren't in evidence. Two, if the reference to 500 is a reference to Mirsad Tokaca, that's got nothing to do with ICMP. And three, this reference to during the last week or two, they came up with the thesis, again there's no basis for that in this case. And if Mr. Karadzic wants to put that case to Mr. Manning, I think we need to see some kind of foundation for it, or he can save it and put it to Dr. Parsons, who will be here in the next couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Could you break down and ask one question at a time with specific and precise reference, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Manning, that to this day the number has not been established and that as time goes by the number is decreasing?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No. If I understand you to mean ICMP's DNA analysis, I'm aware that it has been increasing. I would expect it to increase as they continue their investigation, but if I may, to answer your previous question, I deliberately do not examine the court proceedings and testimony before I'm going to be a witness, so I'm not aware of any of those claims against ICMP or the Bosnian commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the Bosnian commission saying that by mistake some amputees were included in the number of the victims who were dead, whereas these persons are still alive?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Last question. How do you explain this: that at the so-called execution sites -- or, rather, in the graves that are there, there are hundreds and even thousands of shell casings? Does that not indicate that those were the places from where fire was opened and that these were perhaps even trenches, that these were combat positions?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No. In the majority of cases, there's no evidence of a battle being fought in the remote areas where the execution points were, and the evidence from the experts, which I saw myself, was that the shooters stood in a particular area, fired at the victims, and the rounds ejected in a specific area which was either into the grave or collected up when the grave was made or when the grave was robbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the graves and just by the graves, did you find any shell casings? In the graves, too, casings of a large calibre?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: We predominantly found 762 -- 7.62 rounds. We found some shotgun pellets. We found some small-arms rounds. We found one shell case associated with a body at Nova Kasaba 99. We found parts of grenades, and we found what I believe was a part of a rocket propelled grenade within the various graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you explain the fact that there were cases of large-calibre shells in those graves? Who targeted those sites? How did you draw the conclusion that this was a firing position, that there was a fire position from which large-calibre weapons were used to open fire?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was one shell case from an anti-aircraft-style weapon found associated with one body in a shallow grave which we assumed was a gun emplacement. It was the only incident that I can recall of that. The other shell cases, and I physically saw evidence, and I'm aware after having fired the same sort of weapon, that an AK-47 will eject in a certain direction. It will eject to the left of the weapon and the shells will normally land in that direction. When you examine where the shell cases were found, they indicated the shooters were standing in a particular location. Those shell cases were generally ejected to a certain area, and then we would find shell cases amongst the bodies within the grave, in the clothing, within the fill of the grave, perhaps pushed into the grave by heavy machinery, and then transported from one site, the primary grave or execution point, to the secondary grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the forensic summary, May 2000, page 67, it says that 1.031 shell cases were found, and in many places there were tens -- there was a ten or a dozen of them. You found more shell cases than bullets. You found 90 bullet cartridges but you found more shell cases. So my claim is that this wasn't properly investigated and that fire was opened from large-calibre weapons from those positions and trenches were then used in order to bury bodies.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The shell cases referred to, Your Honours, were predominantly 7.62 rounds. They were small shell cases. It's probably the case that a shell case could be a large shell case from an anti-aircraft or tank or similar. That's not what we found. That's not what I was describing. And again, briefly, the archaeologists would establish that it was a rectangular grave with a lamp built by a heavy machine. It was not a fighting trench. That would be very clear. I did not see or read or talk to anyone who indicated that they were defensive trenches in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that an ordinary bullet cartridge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have a stop, otherwise you cannot enter the facility. If absolutely necessary, we can continue, but I am wondering about the quality -- by the line of questioning. I think you exhausted the topic. Do you have re-examination, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd like five minutes, but I don't want to be the difference between keeping the witness here overnight. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We need to stop here. We can't go -- given the Dutch transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we need to finish here, then I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or we can continue tomorrow morning for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No. I'll have nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you mean to put last question? But I think you -- we need to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I was only asking why bullet cartridges were being described as shell cases.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, ballistics expert perhaps would use a different term. A shell case can refer to a small round, it can refer to a big round. It's the casing left over. The bullet is the head. The casing would hold the ammunition, the explosive. It is still correct to call it a shell casing, a bullet shell casing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you all, and in particular, thank you, Mr. Manning. Am I being heard?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I just offer a special thank to Judge Lattanzi, who has had a particularly long day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning, for your coming to The Hague to give your evidence, and I thank all the staff for their kind indulgence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
